mutations.notes: declared equivalent: swap_boolean_condition at redirect.py:29:7 changes `if not parsed.scheme and not parsed.netloc:` to `if not parsed.scheme or not parsed.netloc:` (And -> Or). By the time this line runs, target has already passed the line-18 non-empty-string guard and the line-23 `target.startswith("//")` guard. Given urlparse's grammar, a non-empty netloc can only ever be produced from a scheme-less input by a literal '//' prefix (RFC 3986 authority component requires the '//' marker), and any such input was already rejected at line 23 -- so at line 29, `scheme == ''` implies `netloc == ''` for every surviving input, making the AND and OR conditions identical (both True) whenever scheme is empty. The two conditions can only diverge when scheme is non-empty and netloc is empty (AND is False, OR is True) -- e.g. 'javascript:alert(1)', 'mailto:x@y', 'ftp:foo'. For every such input, urlparse's scheme grammar (ALPHA (ALPHA|DIGIT|+|-|.)*) requires the first character to be alphabetic, so target can never start with '/' when scheme is non-empty. The mutant's newly-entered branch therefore always evaluates `target.startswith("/")` as False and falls through to `raise ValueError("... must be an absolute path")`, while the reference (skipping this branch for the same input) proceeds to line 39's scheme check and raises ValueError there instead (either 'scheme not allowed', or -- for an allowed scheme with no netloc, e.g. 'http:foo' -- 'must have a host' at line 43). Both versions raise ValueError for every input in this class; only the message/line differs, which the contract never specifies. Verified empirically by reconstructing the exact mutant and diffing accept/reject outcome AND exception type against the reference over 60+ probe inputs (all string edge cases: multi-slash, colon-only, scheme-with-empty-netloc, non-string types, case variants, userinfo tricks) -- zero observable differences found, consistent with the proof above.

mutations.notes: declared equivalent: remove_branch_force_false at redirect.py:43:4 disables `if not parsed.netloc: raise ValueError("... must have a host")`. This line is only reached after line 39 has confirmed `parsed.scheme in ("http", "https")`. urlparse's `.hostname` property is derived from `.netloc` and is documented/implemented to return None whenever netloc is empty -- there is no input for which netloc is empty but hostname is non-None. So when this guard's condition is True (netloc empty) and its raise is skipped, execution falls through to line 47: `if parsed.hostname != allowed_host:`, which evaluates `None != allowed_host`. `allowed_host` is a trusted configuration parameter supplied by the calling application (not part of the adversarial `target` input space the task contract defends against) and is always a non-empty hostname string in every case the contract or its hidden/regression suites exercise (e.g. "app.example.com"), so `None != allowed_host` is always True, and the mutant raises ValueError('... does not match allowed host ...') instead of ValueError('... must have a host'). Both are ValueError, for every reachable input (e.g. 'http:foo', 'http:/foo', 'http://', 'https:'), just with a different (contract-unspecified) message. Verified empirically: reconstructed the exact mutant and diffed against the reference over the same 60+ probe input set with allowed_host fixed to a realistic non-empty value -- zero differences in accept/reject outcome or exception type.

controls.name: host_substring_match
controls.description: Matches the host with substring containment (`allowed_host in hostname`) instead of exact equality. Wrongly accepts any host that merely contains the allowed host as a substring, e.g. 'app.example.com.evil.com' -- a domain the attacker fully controls, not just the allowed host itself. A realistic 'looks close enough' mistake when generalizing from a single-example fix.

controls.name: protocol_relative_bypass
controls.description: Checks only `not parsed.scheme` (instead of `not parsed.scheme and not parsed.netloc`) before treating a leading '/' as a safe relative path, and has no explicit pre-check for '//'. Since urlparse('//evil.com') yields an empty scheme, this wrongly classifies the protocol-relative target as relative and returns it unchanged -- a classic open-redirect bypass. Must be rejected by the hidden suite's protocol-relative test.

controls.name: scheme_blacklist
controls.description: Validates the scheme with a blacklist of 'known dangerous' schemes (javascript, data) instead of an allow-list of 'known safe' ones (http, https). Any scheme not on the blacklist -- e.g. 'ftp:' -- slips through to the host check and is wrongly accepted when the host matches. A plausible mistake: fixing the two schemes named in a bug report without generalizing to an allow-list.

controls.name: host_only_scheme_forgotten
controls.description: Security-relevant near-miss reproducing this task's original, since-fixed weakness: validates only the netloc/host and forgets to restrict the URL scheme to http/https. 'javascript://app.example.com/x' and 'data://app.example.com/x' parse with a netloc equal to the allowed host, so they pass the host check and are returned unchanged even though the scheme makes them executable/dangerous. A naive or partial fix that adds host validation without also adding scheme validation would produce exactly this.

controls.name: allowlist_first_dispatch
controls.description: Legitimately different-but-correct implementation: classifies the target into relative-vs-absolute up front via a small predicate helper and a frozenset-based scheme allow-list, rather than the reference's sequential guard clauses. Different control flow and data structure, same accept/reject behavior. Should be ACCEPTED.

findings.summary: A `_pytest/` package nested inside this task's editable subtree is not flagged as a protected-path violation, but empirical testing confirms this is NOT currently exploitable.
findings.detail: Injecting 'saferedirect/_pytest/__init__.py' (nested inside the editable package, not at the snapshot root) was NOT flagged as touching a protected path — but `python -m pytest` never adds the editable package directory itself to sys.path, so this nested `_pytest/` is only importable as `<package>._pytest`, never as the bare top-level `_pytest` the real pytest package needs; a controlled test confirms `import _pytest` still resolves to the real site-packages module. Recorded as a structural gap (no basename/suffix rule catches a directory named `_pytest`) that would only matter if this task ever lost its editable_paths allow-list, not as a live weakness today. See docs/agents/ORACLE.md.

limitations: Grading executes submitted/mutated code via LocalSandbox, which provides per-run workspace isolation and timeouts but NOT untrusted-agent security isolation (runner/afa_runner/sandbox.py's own module docstring). Every check in this report assumes the code being graded is trying to game the SCORE, not attack the HOST — see isolation.hidden_test_readability for a concrete, always-present consequence of that assumption.

Hidden-test readability during grading could not be ruled out (see the isolation.hidden_test_readability check) — this finding is deliberately excluded from the status precedence (afa_integrity.health) because it is a constant, documented property of the current LocalSandbox threat model, not something this specific task can fix.

Mutation equivalence is undecidable in general; a surviving mutant is reported as-is unless explicitly declared equivalent in tasks/<id>/integrity/integrity.json. A mutation kill rate is never treated as a correctness probability (mission §16).
